newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-MATTINGLY, GREATEST YANK NEVER TO SAVOR SERIES, RETIRES.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-MATTINGLY, GREATEST YANK NEVER TO SAVOR SERIES, RETIRES.

text.p: Don Mattingly officially closed the book on a stellar career Wednesday, and his own bittersweet chapter in New York Yankee baseball history.

Mattingly, 35, played his last game in Yankee pinstripes 15 months ago, taking last season off to spend time with his family back home in Indiana and rest his chronically aching back. He had held out the chance of returning to baseball.

A six-time All-Star and nine-time Gold Glove winner at first base, Mattingly said he had been working out last autumn in an attempt to return to the majors, but a series of nagging injuries prompted him to stop his conditioning programme.
"I wasn't ready to go the distance," Mattingly conceded. "When it was time to put more weights on the rack, I was finding reasons to go to the barn. I didn't want to sell out."
Mattingly, a superb first baseman who hit for both power and average, was one of the game's dominant players in the 1980s before back injuries began to sap his skills.
Mattingly's departure at the end of the '95 season provided a melancholy moment for fans, who adored the man who stands alone as perhaps the greatest Yankee never to savor the World Series.
The Yankee captain, who so proudly wore number 23, arrived on the scene one season too late and left one season too early in a cruel twist of timing.
The Yankees, regular visitors to the World Series starting in the 1920 heydays of Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig, fell on hard times at the wrong time for Mattingly.
New York played in the World Series of 1981 and 1996. Mattingly's career stretched from 1982 to 1995.
The Yankees' failure to reach the World Series, however, was no fault of the lefty-swinging first baseman, affectionately known as "Donnie Baseball".
The slightly-built Mattingly generated surprising power to all fields with fast hands whipping the bat out of his coiled, crouched stance.

He won the American League battle title in 1984 with a .343 average. He led the league with 145 RBIs the next season and won Most Valuable Player honours. He set a Yankee record in 1986 with a league-leading 238 hits and nearly repeated as MVP.
After returning from a stop on the disabled list for a disc problem in mid-season of 1987, Mattingly homered in eight consecutive games to set a major league record.
He finished with .307 career average, 222 home runs and 1,099 RBI. In his first six seasons he averaged .327, 203 hits, 27 homers and 114 RBI.
"I'm proud of the everything I accomplished. I look back with joy for having the opportunity and with no regrets," Mattingly said. "When one door closes, another opens."

Mattingly called watching the 1996 World Series a "dual-edged sword," one in which he missed the game but was happy for his former teammates. But he stressed how lucky he was just to play for the Yankees.
"I feel thankful for everything I've been able to do," Mattingly said.
Yankee owner George Steinbrenner praised Mattingly.
"He is the model. Everyone in my eyes will be judged how he compares to him," Steinbrennner said.
Mattingly was saved from being entirely shut out of baseball's playoffs by helping the Yankees win the American League East in his last season.

In the 1995 Division Series against Seattle, Mattingly batted .417 with four doubles and six runs batted as the Yankees fell agonizingly short of advancing after winning the opening two games of the best-of-five series at home.
